concept.concept_description: Narrow the project to a fully formalizable finite-dimensional linear algebra core for CSS codes over `ZMod 2`, avoiding any quotient-dimension theorem that depends on delicate API guesses until the submodule setup is stable. Work with a short chain segment `A --d₂--> B --d₁--> C` satisfying `d₁.comp d₂ = 0`. Define `cycles := LinearMap.ker d₁`, `boundaries := LinearMap.range d₂`, prove `boundaries ≤ cycles`, package the included boundary submodule inside `cycles`, define `homology := cycles ⧸ boundaryInsideCycles`, and then prove a small, concrete theorem ladder in the order most likely supported by Mathlib: (1) the inclusion submodule is well-defined; (2) `FiniteDimensional F cycles`, `FiniteDimensional F boundaries`, and `FiniteDimensional F homology`; (3) `finrank boundaries = finrank (LinearMap.range d₂)` by definitional/rfl-style transport if needed; (4) `finrank cycles + finrank (LinearMap.range d₁) = finrank B` via `LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker`; (5) `finrank homology + finrank boundaryInsideCycles = finrank cycles` via the finite-dimensional quotient formula for submodules; and finally (6) deduce `finrank homology = finrank B - finrank (LinearMap.range d₁) - finrank (LinearMap.range d₂)` using the previous identities and the fact that `boundaryInsideCycles` is linearly equivalent to `range d₂`. If the last subtraction-normalized formula is awkward in `Nat`, it is acceptable to stop at an additive identity such as `finrank homology + finrank (range d₂) + finrank (range d₁) = finrank B`, which is mathematically equivalent and often easier to formalize.
concept.mathematical_framing: The Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error-correcting codes are constructed from classical linear codes C_1, C_2 with C_2 perp subset C_1. The CSS code encodes dim(C_1) - dim(C_2) logical qubits. This is exactly the definition of a cohomology group: H^1(C_1, C_2) = C_1 / C_2. Conjecture: every CSS code is equivalent to a cohomology computation on a simplicial complex, and vice versa. Specifically, given a simplicial complex K, the CSS code with C_1 = Z_1(K, F_2) (1-cycles) and C_2 = B_1(K, F_2) (1-boundaries) encodes dim(H_1(K, F_2)) logical qubits with distance d = min(length of shortest non-trivial cycle, length of shortest non-trivial cocycle). This is the homological quantum error-correcting code HQECC(K). The distance d equals the systole of K (the length of the shortest non-contractible cycle). Conjecture: for the hypercube Q_n (n-dimensional cube graph), the HQECC encodes 1 qubit with distance d = 2^{n/2} (achieving the quantum Singleton bound). Test: construct HQECC for Q_4, Q_6, Q_8 and verify the parameters. Impact: quantum error correction is cohomology. Every simplicial complex gives a quantum code, and the code parameters are topological invariants.

Then H_1(K, F_2) = Z_1/B_1 is the first homology. The CSS code with these C_1, C_2 encodes dim(H_1) qubits. -- NEW_FILE: ab2bf6f4_retry1_aristotle/Catalog/Algebra/HomologicalCSS/Core.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# CSS codes as homology of a finite chain segment over `ZMod 2`

This file formalizes the linear-algebraic dictionary between CSS (Calderbank–Shor–Steane)
quantum codes and the homology of a short chain segment

`A --d₂--> B --d₁--> C`

of finite-dimensional vector spaces over `F := ZMod 2`, with `d₁ ∘ d₂ = 0`.

The *code space* of a CSS code is the quotient of the parity-check kernel
(`cycles := ker d₁`) by the image of the stabilizer generators
(`boundaries := range d₂`).  This is exactly the homology
`homology := cycles ⧸ boundaries` of the chain segment, and its dimension is the
number of logical qubits.

## Main results

* `boundaries_le_cycles` : `range d₂ ≤ ker d₁`, i.e. boundaries are cycles.
* `homology_finrank_eq` : `finrank homology = finrank cycles - finrank boundaries`.
* `finrank_cycles` : `finrank cycles = finrank B - finrank (range d₁)` (rank–nullity).
* `finrank_boundaries` : `finrank boundaries = finrank (range d₂)`.
* `css_dimension_formula` :
  `finrank homology = finrank B - finrank (range d₁) - finrank (range d₂)`.
* `homology_finrank_le` : `finrank homology ≤ finrank B`.

## CSS realization (stretch)

* `css_realization_finrank` : every quotient `C₁ ⧸ C₂` of nested subspaces `C₂ ≤ C₁ ≤ B`
  is the homology of a chain segment, with dimension `finrank C₁ - finrank C₂`.

We work over `F := ZMod 2`, the field relevant to CSS codes; all arguments only use that
`F` is a (finite-dimensional-friendly) field, so they specialize standard Mathlib rank
identities.
-/

namespace HomologicalCSS

open Module

/-- The base field of a CSS code: the binary field. -/
abbrev F := ZMod 2

variable {A B C : Type*}
  [AddCommGroup A] [Module F A] [FiniteDimensional F A]
  [AddCommGroup B] [Module F B] [FiniteDimensional F B]
  [AddCommGroup C] [Module F C] [FiniteDimensional F C]

variable (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)

/-- The cycles of the chain segment: the kernel of the outgoing differential. -/
def cycles : Submodule F B := LinearMap.ker d₁

/-- The boundaries of the chain segment: the image of the incoming differential. -/
def boundaries : Submodule F B := LinearMap.range d₂

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- Boundaries are cycles: `range d₂ ≤ ker d₁`, given `d₁ ∘ d₂ = 0`. -/
theorem boundaries_le_cycles (hcomp : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    boundaries d₂ ≤ cycles d₁ :=
  LinearMap.range_le_ker_iff.mpr hcomp

/-- The boundaries seen as a submodule of the cycles. -/
def boundaryInsideCycles : Submodule F (cycles d₁) :=
  Submodule.comap (cycles d₁).subtype (boundaries d₂)

/-- The homology of the chain segment: cycles modulo boundaries.
This is the CSS code space. -/
abbrev homology : Type _ := (cycles d₁) ⧸ boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The dimension of the boundaries seen inside the cycles equals the dimension of the
boundaries, provided boundaries are cycles. -/
theorem finrank_boundaryInsideCycles (hcomp : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁) = finrank F (boundaries d₂) :=
  (Submodule.comapSubtypeEquivOfLe (boundaries_le_cycles d₂ d₁ hcomp)).finrank_eq

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The homology dimension is the difference of the cycle and boundary dimensions. -/
theorem homology_finrank_eq (hcomp : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (homology d₂ d₁) = finrank F (cycles d₁) - finrank F (boundaries d₂) := by
  have hq := Submodule.finrank_quotient_add_finrank (boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁)
  rw [finrank_boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hcomp] at hq
  show finrank F ((cycles d₁) ⧸ boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁) = _
  omega

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- Rank–nullity for the cycles: `finrank (ker d₁) = finrank B - finrank (range d₁)`. -/
theorem finrank_cycles :
    finrank F (cycles d₁) = finrank F B - finrank F (LinearMap.range d₁) := by
  have h := LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker d₁
  simp only [cycles]
  omega

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The boundary dimension is the rank of the incoming differential. -/
theorem finrank_boundaries :
    finrank F (boundaries d₂) = finrank F (LinearMap.range d₂) := rfl

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The CSS dimension formula: the number of logical qubits is
`finrank B - finrank (range d₁) - finrank (range d₂)`. -/
theorem css_dimension_formula (hcomp : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (homology d₂ d₁) =
      finrank F B - finrank F (LinearMap.range d₁) - finrank F (LinearMap.range d₂) := by
  rw [homology_finrank_eq d₂ d₁ hcomp, finrank_cycles d₁, finrank_boundaries d₂]

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The homology dimension is bounded by the dimension of the middle space. -/
theorem homology_finrank_le (hcomp : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (homology d₂ d₁) ≤ finrank F B := by
  rw [homology_finrank_eq d₂ d₁ hcomp]
  have := Submodule.finrank_le (cycles d₁)
  omega

/-! ## CSS realization

Every quotient `C₁ ⧸ C₂` of nested subspaces `C₂ ≤ C₁` of a finite-dimensional space `B`
arises as the homology of a chain segment, by taking `A := C₂` with `d₂` the inclusion and
`C := B ⧸ C₁` with `d₁` the quotient map. -/

section Realization

variable (C₂ C₁ : Submodule F B)

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- For nested subspaces `C₂ ≤ C₁`, the quotient map after the inclusion is zero. -/
theorem css_chain_comp_zero (h : C₂ ≤ C₁) : (C₁.mkQ).comp (C₂.subtype) = 0 := by
  ext x
  simpa using h x.2

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The cycles of the realizing chain segment are exactly `C₁`. -/
theorem css_cycles_eq : cycles (C₁.mkQ) = C₁ := Submodule.ker_mkQ C₁

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The boundaries of the realizing chain segment are exactly `C₂`. -/
theorem css_boundaries_eq : boundaries (C₂.subtype) = C₂ := Submodule.range_subtype C₂

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The quotient `C₁ ⧸ C₂` is realized as the homology of a chain segment, with dimension
`finrank C₁ - finrank C₂`. -/
theorem css_realization_finrank (h : C₂ ≤ C₁) :
    finrank F (homology (C₂.subtype) (C₁.mkQ)) = finrank F C₁ - finrank F C₂ := by
  rw [homology_finrank_eq _ _ (css_chain_comp_zero C₂ C₁ h),
    css_cycles_eq, css_boundaries_eq]

end Realization

end HomologicalCSS

# Future Directions — CSS Codes as Cohomology

This cycle established the dictionary **CSS code = homology of an `F₂`-chain
complex** (`Core.lean`), *refuted* the hypercube conjecture for the 1-skeleton
cycle code (`CubeCode.lean`), and anchored the refutation with a fully explicit
`[[4,1]]` code on `C₄ = Q₂` (`RingCode.lean`). The surviving topological
invariant is the cyclomatic number `β₁(Q_n) = (n−2)·2^{n-1} + 1`, which equals
`1` **only** at `n = 2`. The directions below grow out of exactly those findings.

---

## Conjecture 1 — The cube becomes a `[[·,1,·]]` code only after filling 2-cells

For the *cubical* complex `Q_n` (vertices, edges **and** square 2-faces), the
homological code has `k = dim H₁(Q_n; F₂) = 0` for `n ≥ 2` (the cube is simply
connected), so to recover a single logical qubit one must quotient/identify
faces into a closed surface. Concretely: there is a surface `Σ` obtained from
`Q_n`'s 2-skeleton with `dim H₁(Σ; F₂) = 1` and code distance equal to the
girth `4`, **not** `2^{n/2}`.

- **The key insight is** that the mission's "1 qubit" claim silently assumes a
  *surface* (2-complex) where 2-cells kill all but one homology class, while the
  literal `Z₁/B₁` cycle code on the 1-skeleton has `B₁ = 0` and therefore
  over-encodes by the full cyclomatic number `(n−2)2^{n-1}+1`.
- **Why now?** `CubeCode.numLogical_graphCode` already isolates the `d₂ = 0`
  (no-2-cell) case; adding a nonzero `d₂` for the square faces is a direct,
  mechanical extension of the same `Core` dimension formula, so the surface vs.
  graph dichotomy is immediately testable in the existing framework.

## Conjecture 2 — Homological distance is governed by Hamming weight, and the cube saturates only the trivial Singleton bound

Define the code distance `d` as the minimum `hammingWeight` (already imported
from the catalog's `vecSupport`) over nonzero homology representatives. Then for
the `C₄` code `d = 4`, and every cube 1-skeleton code has `d = girth = 4`,
giving `k + d = β₁ + 4`, which violates the quantum Singleton bound
`k + 2d ≤ n + 2` for large `n` — i.e. the 1-skeleton codes are **bad** codes,
the opposite of the conjecture's "achieves the Singleton bound" claim.

- **The key insight is** that distance is a *minimum-weight* invariant of the
  cohomology class, so the catalog's `vecSupport_card_pos_of_ne_zero` is the
  exact primitive needed, and the constant girth `4` forces asymptotically
  vanishing relative distance `d/n → 0`.
- **Why now?** `RingCode.ker_boundary` shows the homology class explicitly as a
  single weight-4 vector; computing `hammingWeight` of a kernel basis is already

concept.mathematical_framing: Elementary cellular automata (ECAs) are the 256 rules that update a 1D binary array based on its 3-cell neighborhood. Rule 110 is Turing-complete. Test: compute dim(V(f)) for all 256 ECAs and verify that the dimension correlates with Wolfram's complexity classification (Class 1: dim=0, Class 2: dim<=n/2, Class 3: dim>=n/2, Class 4: dim=n). import Mathlib

/-!
# Elementary Cellular Automata as Algebraic Varieties over GF(2)

An elementary cellular automaton (ECA) updates a cyclic binary array of length `n`
via a local rule `g : GF(2)³ → GF(2)` applied to each cell's 3-neighborhood.  Each of
Wolfram's 256 rules is, by its algebraic normal form (ANF), a polynomial of degree ≤ 3
over `GF(2) = ZMod 2`.  The **fixed-point set** `{s : s = g(s)}` is the GF(2)-variety of
the polynomial system `g(sᵢ₋₁, sᵢ, sᵢ₊₁) = sᵢ`.

The headline conjecture under test claims that the *dimension* (here: log₂ of the number of
fixed configurations) of this variety tracks Wolfram's complexity class — in particular that
the Turing-complete Class-4 Rule 110 should have *maximal* fixed-point dimension `n`.

**Main finding (refutation).**  Rule 110 has *exactly one* fixed point (the all-zero
configuration) for every length `n ≥ 1`, hence fixed-point dimension `0`, while the trivial
identity Rule 204 (Class 2) has all `2ⁿ` configurations fixed (dimension `n`).  So the
Turing-complete rule sits at the *bottom* of the fixed-point-dimension scale, not the top:
the naive "complexity = fixed-point dimension" conjecture is false.

## Results
* `g110_eq_ruleBit` … `g90_eq_ruleBit` : the ANF polynomials really are Wolfram rules 110/204/0/51/90.
* `g110_def_degree3` : Rule 110's ANF `b + c + b·c + a·b·c` is genuinely degree 3.
* `ruleId_isFixed` : every configuration is fixed by Rule 204.
* `rule0_isFixed_iff`, `rule110_isFixed_iff` : `s` is fixed iff `s = 0`.
* `rule51_not_isFixed` : Rule 51 (complement) has no fixed points.
* `rule110_card` , `ruleId_card` : fixed-point counts `1` and `2ⁿ`.
* `complexity_dimension_conjecture_false` : Rule 110 has strictly fewer fixed points than
  the trivial Rule 204 — the refutation.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer).  Seven conjectures were floated; ranked by impact:
  H1*  "Turing-complete ⇒ maximal fixed-point dimension" (Rule 110 ↦ dim n).  [surprising, central]
  H2   Rule 0 / Rule 110 each have a unique fixed point (the all-0 state).
  H3   Identity Rule 204 fixes every configuration (dim n).
  H4   Complement Rule 51 has NO fixed point (empty variety).
  H5*  Linear Rule 90 fixes a GF(2)-subspace whose dimension oscillates with gcd(·,n). [surprising]
  H6   Every rule's ANF is a degree-≤3 GF(2) polynomial (exact correspondence 256↔256).
  H7   Fixed-point count is multiplicative under a transfer matrix: #fix(n) = tr(Tⁿ).

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter).  Brute-force over n = 1..8:
  rule 0  : [1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1]      rule 110: [1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1]
  rule 51 : [0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]      rule 204: [2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256] = 2ⁿ
  rule 90 : [1,1,4,1,1,4,1,1]      (period-3 in n: 4 iff 3 ∣ n)
This immediately FALSIFIES H1: the Turing-complete rule has the *minimum* nonempty
fixed-point count (1), not the maximum (2ⁿ).  H2,H3,H4 confirmed and formalized below.

ANALYSIS (Analyst).  Rule 110 ANF = b + c + bc + abc.  Fixed-point eqn c+bc+abc=0.
  • If sᵢ = 0 the constraint at i forces sᵢ₊₁ = 0  (zero PROPAGATES forward).
  • All-ones is impossible: at a=b=c=1, c+bc+abc = 1+1+1 = 1 ≠ 0.
  Hence some cell is 0, and zero-propagation around the finite cycle forces s ≡ 0.
  The "complexity ↔ dimension" intuition conflates DYNAMICAL richness (transient orbits,
  gliders) with the STATIC fixed-point variety; Turing-completeness lives in the orbits,
  not the equilibria.  Correct invariant would be topological entropy of the *full*
  spacetime SFT, not the fixed-point count.

CRITIQUE (Critic).  Adversarial counterexample search: is there ANY length n where Rule 110
  fixes a nonzero state?  `rule110_isFixed_iff` proves no — robust for all n ≥ 1.  Guard:
  the refutation theorem needs n ≥ 1 (NeZero n) so that 2ⁿ > 1; stated with that hypothesis.

SYNTHESIS (PI).  The fixed-point variety is a genuine GF(2) scheme but its dimension is the
  WRONG complexity invariant.  See FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md for the entropy reformulation.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace ECAFixedVariety

open scoped Classical

/-- A cell value lives in `GF(2) = ZMod 2`. -/
abbrev Cell := ZMod 2

/-- A length-`n` cyclic configuration. -/
abbrev Config (n : ℕ) := ZMod n → Cell

/-- One synchronous ECA update with local rule `g`, on the cyclic array `ZMod n`. -/
def step {n : ℕ} (g : Cell → Cell → Cell → Cell) (s : Config n) : Config n :=
  fun i => g (s (i - 1)) (s i) (s (i + 1))

/-- `s` is a fixed point (an element of the fixed-point variety) of rule `g`. -/
def isFixed {n : ℕ} (g : Cell → Cell → Cell → Cell) (s : Config n) : Prop :=
  step g s = s

/-- Wolfram bit-extraction definition of a rule: output bit number `4a+2b+c` of `r`. -/
def ruleBit (r : ℕ) (a b c : Cell) : Cell :=
  if Nat.testBit r (4 * a.val + 2 * b.val + c.val) then 1 else 0

/-! ### The algebraic normal forms (ANF) of five representative rules. -/

/-- Rule 0: the constant-zero polynomial. -/
def g0 : Cell → Cell → Cell → Cell := fun _ _ _ => 0
/-- Rule 204: identity on the center cell, `f = b`. -/
def gId : Cell → Cell → Cell → Cell := fun _ b _ => b
/-- Rule 51: complement of the center cell, `f = b + 1`. -/
def gNot : Cell → Cell → Cell → Cell := fun _ b _ => b + 1
/-- Rule 90: linear XOR of neighbors, `f = a + c`. -/
def g90 : Cell → Cell → Cell → Cell := fun a _ c => a + c
/-- Rule 110: ANF `f = b + c + b·c + a·b·c` (degree 3). -/
def g110 : Cell → Cell → Cell → Cell := fun a b c => b + c + b * c + a * b * c

/-! ### Faithfulness: the ANF polynomials are exactly the Wolfram rules. -/

theorem g0_eq_ruleBit : ∀ a b c : Cell, g0 a b c = ruleBit 0 a b c := by decide
theorem gId_eq_ruleBit : ∀ a b c : Cell, gId a b c = ruleBit 204 a b c := by decide
theorem gNot_eq_ruleBit : ∀ a b c : Cell, gNot a b c = ruleBit 51 a b c := by decide
theorem g90_eq_ruleBit : ∀ a b c : Cell, g90 a b c = ruleBit 90 a b c := by decide

theorem g110_eq_ruleBit : ∀ a b c : Cell, g110 a b c = ruleBit 110 a b c := by decide

/-- Rule 110's ANF is genuinely degree 3: the top monomial `a·b·c` has coefficient 1,
    witnessed by `g110 1 1 1 = 0 ≠ 1` failing the lower-degree truncation `b + c + b*c`. -/
theorem g110_def_degree3 :
    g110 1 1 1 ≠ (fun _a b c : Cell => b + c + b * c) 1 1 1 := by decide

/-! ### Fixed-point varieties. -/

/-- Rule 204 (identity) fixes *every* configuration: its variety is all of `GF(2)ⁿ`. -/
theorem ruleId_isFixed {n : ℕ} (s : Config n) : isFixed gId s := by
  funext i; rfl

/-
Rule 51 (complement) has an EMPTY fixed-point variety.
-/
theorem rule51_not_isFixed {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (s : Config n) : ¬ isFixed gNot s := by
  intro h; have := congr_fun h 0; simp_all +decide [ isFixed, step ] ;
  unfold gNot at this; aesop;

/-
Rule 0: the only fixed point is the all-zero configuration.
-/
theorem rule0_isFixed_iff {n : ℕ} (s : Config n) : isFixed g0 s ↔ s = 0 := by
  constructor <;> intro h <;> simp_all +decide [ funext_iff, isFixed ];
  · exact fun x => h x ▸ rfl;
  · unfold step g0; aesop;

/-
Zero propagates forward under Rule 110: if cell `i` is `0` then cell `i+1` is `0`.
-/
theorem rule110_zero_propagates {n : ℕ} {s : Config n} (h : isFixed g110 s) (i : ZMod n)
    (hi : s i = 0) : s (i + 1) = 0 := by
      have := congr_fun h i; simp_all +decide [ step, g110 ] ;

/-
**Key theorem.**  The Turing-complete Rule 110 has a UNIQUE fixed point — the all-zero
    configuration — for every length `n ≥ 1`.  Its fixed-point variety is a single point
    (dimension 0), refuting "Turing-complete ⇒ maximal fixed-point dimension".
-/
theorem rule110_isFixed_iff {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (s : Config n) : isFixed g110 s ↔ s = 0 := by
  constructor;
  · intro h_fixed_point
    by_contra h_nonzero;
    obtain ⟨i₀, hi₀⟩ : ∃ i₀ : ZMod n, s i₀ = 0 := by
      by_cases h_all_one : ∀ i : ZMod n, s i = 1;
      · simp_all +decide [ funext_iff, isFixed ];
        specialize h_fixed_point 0 ; simp_all +decide [ step, g110 ];
      · exact not_forall_not.mp fun h => h_all_one fun i => Or.resolve_left ( Fin.exists_fin_two.mp <| by aesop ) <| h i;
    -- By induction on $k$, we show that $s (i₀ + k) = 0$ for all $k$.
    have h_ind : ∀ k : ℕ, s (i₀ + k) = 0 := by
      intro k; induction k <;> simp_all +decide [ ← add_assoc ] ;
      exact rule110_zero_propagates h_fixed_point _ ‹_›;
    refine' h_nonzero ( funext fun x => _ );
    convert h_ind ( ( x - i₀ ) |> ZMod.val ) using 1 ; simp +decide;
  · rintro rfl; unfold isFixed; unfold step; aesop;

/-! ### Counting the GF(2)-points of the varieties. -/

/-
Rule 110's fixed-point variety has exactly one GF(2)-point.
-/
theorem rule110_card {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card {s : Config n // isFixed g110 s} = 1 := by
      rw [ Nat.card_eq_one_iff_unique ];
      exact ⟨ ⟨ fun x y => Subtype.ext <| rule110_isFixed_iff _ |>.1 x.2 ▸ rule110_isFixed_iff _ |>.1 y.2 ▸ rfl ⟩, ⟨ 0, ( rule110_isFixed_iff 0 ).mpr rfl ⟩ ⟩

/-
Rule 204's fixed-point variety is all of `GF(2)ⁿ`, with `2ⁿ` points.
-/
theorem ruleId_card {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card {s : Config n // isFixed gId s} = 2 ^ n := by
      -- Since every configuration is fixed by gId, the set of fixed points is equivalent to the set of all configurations.
      have h_equiv : {s : Config n | isFixed gId s} = Set.univ := by
        exact Set.eq_univ_of_forall fun s => ruleId_isFixed s;
      rw [ show { s : Config n // isFixed gId s } = { s : Config n | isFixed gId s } from rfl, h_equiv, Nat.card_eq_fintype_card ] ; simp +decide [ Fintype.card_pi ]

/-
**Refutation of the central conjecture.**  For every length `n ≥ 1`, the Turing-complete
    (Wolfram Class 4) Rule 110 has STRICTLY FEWER fixed configurations than the trivial
    identity Rule 204 (Class 2).  Complexity does not equal fixed-point dimension.
-/
theorem complexity_dimension_conjecture_false {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card {s : Config n // isFixed g110 s} < Nat.card {s : Config n // isFixed gId s} := by
  rw [ rule110_card, ruleId_card ];
  exact one_lt_pow₀ ( by decide ) ( NeZero.ne n )

end ECAFixedVariety

import Computation.ECAFixedVariety

/-!
# Linear Elementary Cellular Automata: the Fixed-Point Variety is a GF(2)-Subspace

This file refines the variety picture of `Computation.ECAFixedVariety` for the *additive*
(GF(2)-linear) ECA rules — those whose algebraic normal form is `f = α·a + β·b + γ·c` with
`α, β, γ ∈ GF(2)` and no constant term.  For these rules the global update map is a
GF(2)-linear endomorphism of `Config n = (ZMod n → ZMod 2)`, so its fixed-point set is the
kernel of the linear map `step − id` — a genuine vector subspace, and hence its number of
GF(2)-points is a power of two.

The leading example is **Rule 90** (`f = a + c`, the neighbor XOR), the canonical linear ECA
producing the Sierpiński triangle.

## Results
* `lstep` : the linear-rule update packaged as a `ZMod 2`-linear map `Config n →ₗ Config n`.
* `linearFixed` : the fixed-point set of a linear rule, as a `Submodule (ZMod 2) (Config n)`.
* `linearFixed_card_pow_two` : that variety has `2 ^ k` points for some `k` (it is a subspace).
* `g90_is_linear` : Rule 90's ANF equals `lstep 1 0 1` (it is linear).
* `g110_not_linear` : Rule 110 is **not** of this linear form (no `(α,β,γ)` reproduces its
  cubic ANF), separating it from the additive rules.
* `rule90_nontrivial_fixed_three` : at `n = 3` Rule 90 has a *nonzero* fixed configuration,
  so its variety has dimension ≥ 1 — strictly larger than Rule 110's single point.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer).  H5: for a *linear* rule the fixed-point variety is a GF(2)
  subspace, so its size is always a power of two, and for Rule 90 the dimension oscillates
  with `gcd`-type number theory in `n`.  This is the algebraic-geometry intuition done right:
  linear rules ↦ linear varieties (affine subspaces), in contrast to the genuinely nonlinear
  Rule 110 whose degree-3 ANF gives a non-subspace variety.

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter).  Rule 90 counts (n=1..8): 1,1,4,1,1,4,1,1 — a clean period-3
  pattern: `#fix = 4` exactly when `3 ∣ n`, else `1`.  All counts are powers of two, matching
  the subspace prediction; the witness `s3 = (1,1,0)` realizes the nonzero fixed state at n=3.
  By contrast Rule 110's fixed set is constantly the single point 0, and Rule 110 is provably
  nonlinear — so the "power of two" guarantee comes specifically from linearity.

ANALYSIS (Analyst).  The map `lstep α β γ : Config n → Config n`,
  `s ↦ (i ↦ α·s(i−1) + β·s i + γ·s(i+1))`, is additive and `ZMod 2`-homogeneous, hence
  `LinearMap`.  `isFixed = (lstep = id) = ker (lstep − id)`, a `Submodule`.  Over the finite
  field `GF(2)` every finite-dimensional subspace has `2^(finrank)` elements, explaining the
  powers of two.  Rule 110 is excluded because its ANF carries the genuinely cubic monomial
  `a·b·c`, so its update is not additive (see `g110_not_linear`).

CRITIQUE (Critic).  Adversarial check: is EVERY rule with a power-of-two fixed-count linear?
  No — the converse fails (Rule 0 and Rule 110 both give count 1 = 2⁰ yet 110 is nonlinear),
  so "power of two" is necessary-from-linearity but not sufficient-for-linearity.  We therefore
  state the implication in the safe direction only and certify Rule 110's nonlinearity directly.

SYNTHESIS (PI).  Linear ECAs are exactly the ones whose fixed-point scheme is a linear
  subscheme; their "dimension" (= finrank) is the honest algebraic invariant.  The nonlinear
  rules (e.g. 110) need the spacetime-SFT entropy invariant proposed in FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace ECALinearSubspace

open ECAFixedVariety
open scoped Classical

/-- The update map of a linear rule `f = α·a + β·b + γ·c`, as a bare function. -/
def lstepFun {n : ℕ} (α β γ : Cell) (s : Config n) : Config n :=
  fun i => α * s (i - 1) + β * s i + γ * s (i + 1)

/-- The linear-rule update packaged as a `ZMod 2`-linear endomorphism of `Config n`. -/
def lstep {n : ℕ} (α β γ : Cell) : Config n →ₗ[ZMod 2] Config n where
  toFun := lstepFun α β γ
  map_add' s t := by
    funext i; simp only [lstepFun, Pi.add_apply]; ring
  map_smul' c s := by
    funext i; simp only [lstepFun, Pi.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul, RingHom.id_apply]; ring

theorem lstep_apply {n : ℕ} (α β γ : Cell) (s : Config n) (i : ZMod n) :
    lstep α β γ s i = α * s (i - 1) + β * s i + γ * s (i + 1) := rfl

/-- The fixed-point set of a linear rule, as a genuine `ZMod 2`-subspace of `Config n`:
    it is the kernel of the linear map `lstep − id`. -/
def linearFixed {n : ℕ} (α β γ : Cell) : Submodule (ZMod 2) (Config n) :=
  LinearMap.ker (lstep α β γ - LinearMap.id)

/-- Membership in the linear fixed-point subspace is exactly being a fixed point. -/
theorem mem_linearFixed {n : ℕ} (α β γ : Cell) (s : Config n) :
    s ∈ linearFixed α β γ ↔ lstepFun α β γ s = s := by
  rw [linearFixed, LinearMap.mem_ker, LinearMap.sub_apply, LinearMap.id_apply, sub_eq_zero]
  exact Iff.rfl

/-- **Structure theorem.**  The fixed-point variety of a linear rule has `2 ^ k`
    GF(2)-points for some `k` (it is a finite-dimensional `GF(2)`-subspace). -/
theorem linearFixed_card_pow_two {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (α β γ : Cell) :
    ∃ k : ℕ, Nat.card (linearFixed α β γ : Submodule (ZMod 2) (Config n)) = 2 ^ k := by
  refine ⟨Module.finrank (ZMod 2) (linearFixed α β γ : Submodule (ZMod 2) (Config n)), ?_⟩
  rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Module.card_eq_pow_finrank (K := ZMod 2)]
  norm_num

/-- Rule 90 (neighbor XOR `f = a + c`) is the linear rule `lstep 1 0 1`. -/
theorem g90_is_linear {n : ℕ} (s : Config n) :
    step g90 s = lstepFun 1 0 1 s := by
  funext i; simp only [step, g90, lstepFun]; ring

/-- Rule 110 is **not** linear: there is no `(α, β, γ)` for which its ANF matches
    `α·a + β·b + γ·c`.  Evaluating any such linear form at `(0,1,0)` and `(0,0,1)` forces
    `β = γ = 1`, but then it gives `0` at `(0,1,1)` whereas `g110 0 1 1 = 1` — the cubic ANF
    breaks additivity. -/
theorem g110_not_linear :
    ¬ ∃ α β γ : Cell, ∀ a b c : Cell, g110 a b c = α * a + β * b + γ * c := by
  rintro ⟨α, β, γ, h⟩
  have h1 := h 0 1 0
  have h2 := h 0 0 1
  have h3 := h 0 1 1
  revert h1 h2 h3
  revert α β γ
  decide

/-! ### A nonzero point of Rule 90's variety: dimension ≥ 1 at `n = 3`. -/

/-- Explicit nonzero fixed configuration of Rule 90 at length 3: `s3 = (1, 1, 0)`. -/
def s3 : Config 3 := ![1, 1, 0]

/-- At length `n = 3`, Rule 90's fixed-point variety contains a **nonzero** point, so it has
    dimension ≥ 1 — strictly larger than Rule 110's single-point variety.  This realizes the
    `#fix = 4 = 2²` count at `n = 3` from the experiment. -/
theorem rule90_nontrivial_fixed_three : isFixed g90 s3 ∧ s3 ≠ 0 := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · funext i; fin_cases i <;> decide
  · intro h; have := congrFun h 0; simp [s3] at this

end ECALinearSubspace

# Chip-Firing and Divisor Theory on a Finite Graph — Definitions

This file lays the *load-bearing foundation* of Baker–Norine divisor theory on a finite
graph, working entirely over an ordinary Mathlib `SimpleGraph V`.

The central object is the **graph Laplacian** (chip-firing operator)

  `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`,

a map `(V → ℤ) → Divisor V`.  We record here the definitions (`Divisor`, `lap`,
`divisorDegree`, `genus`, `canonicalDivisor`, `Effective`, `singleVertexDivisor`,
`bnNumber`) together with the *homomorphism layer*: `lap` is additive, kills constants,
respects negation, and lands in degree zero.  These five facts are exactly the axioms
needed to make chip-firing (linear) equivalence an `Equivalence` and degree a class
invariant (developed in `Tropical.ChipFiring.Theorems`).

## References

* Baker, M. and Norine, S. "Riemann–Roch and Abel–Jacobi theory on a finite graph" (2007)

-- !-- Lab Notebook -- !--
Hypothesis: The whole algebraic layer of divisor theory is the *coset relation of one
  homomorphism* `lap`.  If `lap` is an additive, constant-killing, degree-zero map then
  linear equivalence and its degree invariance must follow purely formally.
Result: Confirmed.  `lap_zero`/`lap_neg`/`lap_add` are literally the three
  equivalence-relation axioms; `lap_deg_zero` is literally degree invariance.
Insight: `lap_deg_zero` needs *no* handshake/degree counting — it is pure antisymmetry of
  `f v − f u` under the symmetric adjacency relation, witnessed by a single
  `Finset.sum_nbij'` swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` that negates every summand.
Failure analysis: Earlier encodings (a weighted multigraph `V → V → ℤ` carrying explicit
  symmetry, and a `deg(v)·f v − ∑ f u` Laplacian) obscured the antisymmetry that does all
  the work; the clean `∑_{u∼v}(f v − f u)` form makes the swap argument immediate.
-- !-- end -- !--
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset BigOperators SimpleGraph

/-! ## Divisors -/

/-- A divisor on a graph with vertex set `V` is an integer-valued function on vertices
(a formal `ℤ`-linear combination of vertices). -/
structure Divisor (V : Type*) where
  coeff : V → ℤ

namespace Divisor
variable {V : Type*}

@[ext] lemma ext {D E : Divisor V} (h : D.coeff = E.coeff) : D = E := by
  cases D; cases E; simpa using h

instance : Zero (Divisor V) := ⟨⟨fun _ => 0⟩⟩
instance : Add (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v + E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Neg (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D => ⟨fun v => -D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Sub (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v - E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℕ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℤ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩

@[simp] lemma zero_coeff (v : V) : (0 : Divisor V).coeff v = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma add_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D + E).coeff v = D.coeff v + E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma neg_coeff (D : Divisor V) (v : V) : (-D).coeff v = -D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma sub_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D - E).coeff v = D.coeff v - E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma nsmul_coeff (n : ℕ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma zsmul_coeff (n : ℤ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl

/-- The coefficient projection `Divisor V → (V → ℤ)` is injective; hence divisors form an
additive commutative group under pointwise operations. -/
instance : AddCommGroup (Divisor V) :=
  Function.Injective.addCommGroup (Divisor.coeff)
    (fun _ _ h => Divisor.ext h)
    rfl (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)
    (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)

end Divisor

/-- A divisor is **effective** when every coefficient is non-negative. -/
def Effective {V : Type*} (D : Divisor V) : Prop := ∀ v, 0 ≤ D.coeff v

/-! ## Degree -/

section Degree
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V]

/-- The **degree** of a divisor is the sum of its coefficients. -/
def divisorDegree (D : Divisor V) : ℤ := ∑ v, D.coeff v

@[simp] lemma divisorDegree_zero : divisorDegree (0 : Divisor V) = 0 := by
  simp [divisorDegree]

lemma divisorDegree_add (D E : Divisor V) :
    divisorDegree (D + E) = divisorDegree D + divisorDegree E := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_add_distrib]

lemma divisorDegree_neg (D : Divisor V) : divisorDegree (-D) = -divisorDegree D := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_neg_distrib]

end Degree

/-! ## The graph Laplacian (chip-firing operator) -/

section Laplacian
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- The graph Laplacian applied to a firing pattern `f : V → ℤ`.  Firing along `f` moves
chips according to `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`. -/
def lap (f : V → ℤ) : Divisor V := ⟨fun v => ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u)⟩

@[simp] lemma lap_coeff (f : V → ℤ) (v : V) :
    (lap G f).coeff v = ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u) := rfl

-- !-- The empty firing pattern moves no chips: each summand `0 - 0` vanishes. -- !--
@[simp] theorem lap_zero : lap G (0 : V → ℤ) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- A constant firing pattern is in the kernel: every summand `c - c` vanishes. -- !--
theorem lap_const (c : ℤ) : lap G (fun _ => c) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- Additivity: `(f+g)v - (f+g)u = (f v - f u) + (g v - g u)`, then split the sum. -- !--
theorem lap_add (f g : V → ℤ) : lap G (f + g) = lap G f + lap G g := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.add_coeff, Pi.add_apply, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Negation: `lap` is `ℤ`-linear, so it commutes with pointwise negation. -- !--
theorem lap_neg (f : V → ℤ) : lap G (-f) = - lap G f := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.neg_coeff, Pi.neg_apply, ← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Every Laplacian has degree zero, by antisymmetry of `f v - f u` under the symmetric
--     adjacency relation: the swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` on adjacent ordered pairs negates each
--     summand yet preserves the index set, forcing `X = -X`. -- !--
theorem lap_deg_zero (f : V → ℤ) : divisorDegree (lap G f) = 0 := by
  unfold divisorDegree
  simp only [lap_coeff]
  have key : (∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u))
      = ∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f u - f v) := by
    rw [Finset.sum_sigma', Finset.sum_sigma']
    apply Finset.sum_nbij' (fun x => (⟨x.2, x.1⟩ : Σ _ : V, V)) (fun x => ⟨x.2, x.1⟩)
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl
  have hneg : (∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f u - f v))
      = -(∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u)) := by
    rw [← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]; apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro v _
    rw [← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]; apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring
  have := key.trans hneg
  linarith

/-! ## Genus and the canonical divisor -/

/-- The (combinatorial) **genus** of a graph: `g = |E| − |V| + 1`, the first Betti number. -/
def genus : ℤ := (G.edgeFinset.card : ℤ) - (Fintype.card V : ℤ) + 1

/-- The **canonical divisor** assigns to each vertex `deg(v) − 2`. -/
def canonicalDivisor : Divisor V := ⟨fun v => (G.degree v : ℤ) - 2⟩

end Laplacian

/-! ## Single-vertex divisors -/

section Single
variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V]

/-- The divisor `k·[v₀]` placing `k` chips on `v₀` and none elsewhere. -/
def singleVertexDivisor (v₀ : V) (k : ℤ) : Divisor V :=
  ⟨fun w => if w = v₀ then k else 0⟩

end Single

/-! ## The Brill–Noether number -/

/-- The **Brill–Noether number** `ρ(g,r,d) = g − (r+1)(g − d + r)`. -/
def bnNumber (g r d : ℤ) : ℤ := g - (r + 1) * (g - d + r)

- `rule110_card = 1`, `ruleId_card = 2ⁿ`, and `complexity_dimension_conjecture_false`: **the central conjecture is refuted** — the Turing-complete Class-4 Rule 110 has strictly fewer fixed points (dimension 0) than the trivial identity Rule 204, so "complexity = fixed-point dimension" is false.

**`Catalog/Computation/ECALinearSubspace.lean`** — refines the picture for linear (additive) rules, building on the first file. Results:

# Future Directions — Cellular Automata as Algebraic Geometry over GF(2)

These conjectures are distilled from the v16a research cycle in
`Computation/ECAFixedVariety.lean` and `Computation/ECALinearSubspace.lean`.

The cycle established two anchor facts:

* **Refutation.** The Turing-complete Wolfram Rule 110 has a *single* fixed point
  (the all-zero configuration) for every length `n ≥ 1`, hence fixed-point-variety
  dimension `0` — the *minimum* among nonempty varieties — directly falsifying the
  conjecture "Turing-complete ⇒ maximal fixed-point dimension"
  (`complexity_dimension_conjecture_false`).
* **Structure.** For *linear* (additive) rules the fixed-point set is literally the
  kernel of `step − id`, a `GF(2)`-subspace, so it always has `2^k` points
  (`linearFixed_card_pow_two`); Rule 110 is provably nonlinear (`g110_not_linear`).

The fixed-point variety is therefore a real GF(2) scheme, but its dimension is the
*wrong* complexity invariant. The directions below propose the right one.

---

## Direction 1 — Spacetime entropy, not fixed-point dimension, tracks complexity.

**Conjecture.** Define the *spacetime subshift* `Σ_r` of rule `r` as the set of valid
bi-infinite orbit diagrams, an SFT over the de Bruijn graph. Its topological entropy
`h(Σ_r) = lim (1/n) log #(period-n columns)` separates Wolfram's classes:
`h = 0` for Class 1/2, `h > 0` for Class 3, and Class 4 (e.g. Rule 110) sits exactly
at the `h = 0` boundary while supporting unbounded transients.

**The key insight is** that Turing-completeness lives in the *transient orbit
structure* (gliders, collisions), which the static fixed-point variety throws away;
the spacetime SFT retains it and its entropy is the genuine invariant.

**Why now?** This cycle proved the fixed-point count of Rule 110 is constantly `1`,
so any complexity invariant *must* be orbit-based, not equilibrium-based. The
transfer-matrix machinery for counting period-`n` configurations (`tr(T^n)`) is
already formalizable in Mathlib (`Matrix.trace`, `Matrix.pow`), giving an immediate
attack route.

## Direction 2 — Fixed-point count is `tr(Tᵣⁿ)` for a 4×4 GF(2)-transfer matrix.

**Conjecture.** For every rule `r` there is an explicit `0/1` matrix `T_r` indexed by
2-cell windows such that `Nat.card {s : Config n // isFixed (g r) s} = trace (T_rⁿ)`,
and the asymptotic growth rate equals the Perron eigenvalue `ρ(T_r)`; the variety
"dimension" is `log₂ ρ(T_r)`, a rule-intrinsic real number.

**The key insight is** that the fixed-point set is a *subshift of finite type*, so its
cardinality is governed by a transfer matrix exactly as in statistical mechanics —
turning a combinatorial count into linear algebra.

**Why now?** We verified the pattern computationally (Rule 90: `1,1,4,1,1,4,…`,
period-3 because `ρ` has a cube-root-of-unity spectrum; Rule 204: `2^n` because
`ρ = 2`). Proving `#fix = tr(Tⁿ)` for the five formalized rules is a finite, bounded
target that would convert every numeric observation in the Lab Notes into a theorem.

## Direction 3 — `3 ∣ n ⇔ Rule 90 has a nonzero fixed point`.

**Conjecture.** The Rule 90 fixed-point subspace `linearFixed 1 0 1` over `Config n`
has dimension `> 0` if and only if `3 ∣ n`; equivalently the circulant operator
`x ↦ x_{i-1} + x_{i+1} − x_i` is singular over `GF(2)` exactly when `3 ∣ n`. More
generally the dimension equals `deg gcd(t² + t + 1, tⁿ − 1)` in `GF(2)[t]`.

**The key insight is** that a linear ECA's fixed-point dimension is a *cyclotomic*
quantity: it counts roots of the rule's characteristic polynomial among the `n`-th
roots of unity, so number theory (orders mod small primes) governs the geometry.

**Why now?** We proved a nonzero fixed point exists at `n = 3`
(`rule90_nontrivial_fixed_three`) and `linearFixed_card_pow_two` already exposes the
dimension as `finrank`. Mathlib's `Polynomial.cyclotomic` and circulant-matrix
support make the gcd characterization directly reachable.

## Direction 4 — Linearity is *decidable from the variety* up to the converse gap.

**Conjecture.** A rule `r` is GF(2)-linear iff its fixed-point variety is closed under
addition for *all* lengths `n` simultaneously; a single length can fail (the converse
gap noted by the Critic: Rule 0 and Rule 110 both give count `1 = 2⁰` yet only Rule 0
is linear). Precisely: `(∀ n, IsSubmodule (fixed r n)) ↔ r ∈ {0,60,90,102,150,170,204,240,…}`
(the 8 additive rules and their reflections).

**The key insight is** that linearity is a *global* property of the whole tower of
varieties `{V_n}`, not of any single `V_n` — closure-at-one-`n` is necessary but not
sufficient, which is why our safe-direction lemma (`g110_not_linear`) certifies
nonlinearity pointwise rather than from a single count.

**Why now?** This cycle isolated the exact converse counterexample (count `1` is
realized by both a linear and a nonlinear rule), so the precise boundary is known and
ready to be formalized as an `Iff` over the finite catalogue of additive rules.

## Direction 5 — Affine rules give *cosets*; the empty variety detects an inhomogeneity.

**Conjecture.** A rule with affine ANF `f = ℓ(a,b,c) + 1` (a linear part plus the
constant `1`, e.g. Rule 51 `= b + 1`) has fixed-point variety either empty or a
*coset* of `linearFixed ℓ`; it is empty exactly when `1 ∉ image(ℓ − id)`. Thus the
empty variety (`rule51_not_isFixed`) is the GF(2) shadow of an unsolvable affine
system, and `#fix ∈ {0} ∪ {2^k}`.

**The key insight is** that the constant term in the ANF turns the *kernel* (subspace)
into an *affine* solution set, so the dichotomy "empty vs. power-of-two coset" is the
Rouché–Capelli theorem over `GF(2)` applied to cellular automata.

**Why now?** We already proved Rule 51's variety is empty for all `n`; recasting that
as the inconsistency of an affine GF(2) system, via Mathlib's `LinearMap.range` and
coset API, would unify the linear (Direction 1–3) and degenerate cases under one
solvability criterion.

concept.title: Sperner's Lemma Implies Nash Equilibria: Combinatorial Fixed Points in Game Theory
concept.concept_description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. This is a combinatorial analog of Brouwer's fixed point theorem. Nash's theorem states that every finite game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, proved using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Conjecture: Sperner's lemma directly implies Nash's theorem. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.

Define Sperner coloring c: Delta -> {1, ..., n} by c(v) = i where i = argmax_j BR_i(v)_j (player i's best response to v has highest probability on strategy j). Boundary condition: if v is on the face where p_i = 0, then c(v) != i (a player with zero probability cannot have a best response there). Wait, the correct boundary condition is: if v is on the face where v_i = 0, then c(v) is not i. Sperner's lemma: there exists at least one fully colored simplex (with all colors 1, ..., n). The center of this simplex is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium where epsilon depends on the mesh size of the triangulation. As mesh -> 0, epsilon -> 0, giving an exact Nash equilibrium. Algorithm: triangulate Delta with mesh epsilon, color vertices by best responses, find fully colored simplex by Sperner's lemma (using the path-following algorithm). Complexity: O((1/epsilon)^{n-1} * |S|) per iteration. Test: implement for 2x2 games (Matching Pennies, Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes). Verify that the algorithm finds the unique Nash equilibrium.

/-
# Finite reconstruction from the specialization relation

This file develops the *finite reconstruction theorem*: on a finite type, a
topology is completely determined by its specialization relation `⤳`.

We work with mathlib's existing notions throughout:

* `x ⤳ y` is `Specializes x y` (`x` specializes to `y`, i.e. `𝓝 x ≤ 𝓝 y`).
* Finite types are automatically Alexandrov-discrete
  (`Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete`), which is what powers the converse direction.
* The "topology generated by a preorder" is mathlib's lower set topology
  `Topology.lowerSet`, whose open sets are exactly the lower sets.  With this
  convention the specialization relation matches the order directly:
  `a ⤳ b ↔ a ≤ b` (`Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le`).

## Main results

* `isOpen_specializes_down` : every open set is downward closed under
  specialization (valid for an arbitrary topology).
* `isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite` : on a finite type the converse holds, so
  openness is *characterized* by being downward closed under specialization.
* `topology_eq_of_specializes_iff_finite` : **the main deliverable** — two
  topologies on a finite type with the same specialization relation are equal.
* `specializes_preorderTopology_iff` : the specialization relation of the lower
  set topology of a preorder recovers the preorder exactly.
* `specPreorder_lowerSet_eq` / `lowerSet_specPreorder_eq_finite` : a pair of
  inverse theorems on finite spaces.

## Sanity checks

* `specializes_discrete_iff` : the discrete topology has trivial specialization.
* `specPreorder_lowerSet_eq` : the lower set topology recovers its preorder.
-/

import Mathlib

open Topology

namespace FiniteSpecialization

variable {α : Type*}

/-! ### Goal 1: open sets are downward closed under specialization -/

/-- For an arbitrary topology, every open set is downward closed under
specialization: if `a ∈ s` and `b ⤳ a` then `b ∈ s`.

This is exactly `IsOpen.stableUnderGeneralization`, restated in the requested
shape using `specializes_iff_forall_open`. -/
theorem isOpen_specializes_down {t : TopologicalSpace α} {s : Set α}
    (hs : IsOpen s) : ∀ ⦃a b⦄, a ∈ s → b ⤳ a → b ∈ s :=
  fun _ _ ha hba => (specializes_iff_forall_open.mp hba) s hs ha

/-! ### Goal 2: the finite converse -/

/-- **Characterization of openness on a finite type.**  A set `s` is open iff it
is downward closed under specialization.

The forward direction is `isOpen_specializes_down`; the converse uses that finite
types are Alexandrov-discrete (`Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete`), where openness is
equivalent to stability under generalization
(`isOpen_iff_forall_specializes`).  The minimal open neighborhood of a point `a`
referenced in the informal strategy is mathlib's `nhdsKer {a}`, the kernel of the
neighborhood filter, i.e. the intersection of all open neighborhoods of `a`. -/
theorem isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite [Fintype α] [TopologicalSpace α]
    (s : Set α) : IsOpen s ↔ ∀ ⦃a b⦄, a ∈ s → b ⤳ a → b ∈ s := by
  rw [isOpen_iff_forall_specializes]
  exact ⟨fun h a b ha hba => h b a hba ha, fun h x y hxy hy => h hy hxy⟩

/-! ### Goal 3: extensionality from specialization (main deliverable) -/

/-- **Finite reconstruction theorem.**  Two topologies on a finite type that have
the same specialization relation pointwise are equal.

The proof is extensionality on open sets: by
`isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite` openness of a set under either topology is
characterized purely by the specialization relation, which agrees by hypothesis. -/
theorem topology_eq_of_specializes_iff_finite [Fintype α] (t₁ t₂ : TopologicalSpace α)
    (h : ∀ a b : α, (@Specializes α t₁ a b ↔ @Specializes α t₂ a b)) : t₁ = t₂ := by
  haveI : @AlexandrovDiscrete α t₁ := @Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete α t₁ _
  haveI : @AlexandrovDiscrete α t₂ := @Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete α t₂ _
  apply TopologicalSpace.ext
  ext s
  rw [@isOpen_iff_forall_specializes α t₁ _ s, @isOpen_iff_forall_specializes α t₂ _ s]
  exact ⟨fun H x y hxy hy => H x y ((h x y).mpr hxy) hy,
         fun H x y hxy hy => H x y ((h x y).mp hxy) hy⟩

/-! ### Goal 4: the preorder topology recovers the preorder -/

/-- The specialization relation of the lower set topology of a preorder recovers
the order exactly.

Orientation note: with mathlib's lower set topology (open sets = lower sets) the
specialization relation satisfies `a ⤳ b ↔ a ≤ b`
(`Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le`).  (For the *upper* set topology, used
by mathlib's `specializationPreorder`, the convention is reversed:
`a ⤳ b ↔ b ≤ a`.) -/
theorem specializes_preorderTopology_iff [Preorder α] (a b : α) :
    @Specializes α (Topology.lowerSet α) a b ↔ a ≤ b := by
  letI := Topology.lowerSet α
  haveI : Topology.IsLowerSet α := ⟨rfl⟩
  exact Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le

/-! ### Sanity check -/

/-- Sanity check: the discrete topology has trivial specialization. -/
theorem specializes_discrete_iff [TopologicalSpace α] [DiscreteTopology α] (a b : α) :
    a ⤳ b ↔ a = b := specializes_iff_eq

/-! ### Goal 5: a pair of inverse theorems on finite spaces -/

/-- The specialization preorder of a topology, in the lower-set orientation
`a ≤ b ↔ a ⤳ b`.  (This is the order-dual of mathlib's `specializationPreorder`,
chosen so that it pairs with the lower set topology above.) -/
def specPreorder (t : TopologicalSpace α) : Preorder α where
  le a b := a ⤳ b
  le_refl a := specializes_refl a
  le_trans _ _ _ hab hbc := hab.trans hbc

@[simp] theorem specPreorder_le_iff (t : TopologicalSpace α) (a b : α) :
    (specPreorder t).le a b ↔ a ⤳ b := Iff.rfl

/-- Inverse 1 (preorder → topology → preorder): starting from a preorder, the
specialization preorder of its lower set topology recovers the original order. -/
theorem specPreorder_lowerSet_eq [Preorder α] (a b : α) :
    (specPreorder (Topology.lowerSet α)).le a b ↔ a ≤ b :=
  specializes_preorderTopology_iff a b

/-- Inverse 2 (topology → preorder → topology): on a finite type, the lower set
topology of the specialization preorder recovers the original topology. -/
theorem lowerSet_specPreorder_eq_finite [Fintype α] (t : TopologicalSpace α) :
    @Topology.lowerSet α (specPreorder t) = t := by
  apply topology_eq_of_specializes_iff_finite
  intro a b
  rw [@specializes_preorderTopology_iff α (specPreorder t) a b]
  rfl

end FiniteSpecialization

# Chip-Firing and Divisor Theory on a Finite Graph — Definitions

This file lays the *load-bearing foundation* of Baker–Norine divisor theory on a finite
graph, working entirely over an ordinary Mathlib `SimpleGraph V`.

The central object is the **graph Laplacian** (chip-firing operator)

  `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`,

a map `(V → ℤ) → Divisor V`.  We record here the definitions (`Divisor`, `lap`,
`divisorDegree`, `genus`, `canonicalDivisor`, `Effective`, `singleVertexDivisor`,
`bnNumber`) together with the *homomorphism layer*: `lap` is additive, kills constants,
respects negation, and lands in degree zero.  These five facts are exactly the axioms
needed to make chip-firing (linear) equivalence an `Equivalence` and degree a class
invariant (developed in `Tropical.ChipFiring.Theorems`).

## References

* Baker, M. and Norine, S. "Riemann–Roch and Abel–Jacobi theory on a finite graph" (2007)

-- !-- Lab Notebook -- !--
Hypothesis: The whole algebraic layer of divisor theory is the *coset relation of one
  homomorphism* `lap`.  If `lap` is an additive, constant-killing, degree-zero map then
  linear equivalence and its degree invariance must follow purely formally.
Result: Confirmed.  `lap_zero`/`lap_neg`/`lap_add` are literally the three
  equivalence-relation axioms; `lap_deg_zero` is literally degree invariance.
Insight: `lap_deg_zero` needs *no* handshake/degree counting — it is pure antisymmetry of
  `f v − f u` under the symmetric adjacency relation, witnessed by a single
  `Finset.sum_nbij'` swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` that negates every summand.
Failure analysis: Earlier encodings (a weighted multigraph `V → V → ℤ` carrying explicit
  symmetry, and a `deg(v)·f v − ∑ f u` Laplacian) obscured the antisymmetry that does all
  the work; the clean `∑_{u∼v}(f v − f u)` form makes the swap argument immediate.
-- !-- end -- !--
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset BigOperators SimpleGraph

/-! ## Divisors -/

/-- A divisor on a graph with vertex set `V` is an integer-valued function on vertices
(a formal `ℤ`-linear combination of vertices). -/
structure Divisor (V : Type*) where
  coeff : V → ℤ

namespace Divisor
variable {V : Type*}

@[ext] lemma ext {D E : Divisor V} (h : D.coeff = E.coeff) : D = E := by
  cases D; cases E; simpa using h

instance : Zero (Divisor V) := ⟨⟨fun _ => 0⟩⟩
instance : Add (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v + E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Neg (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D => ⟨fun v => -D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Sub (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v - E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℕ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℤ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩

@[simp] lemma zero_coeff (v : V) : (0 : Divisor V).coeff v = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma add_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D + E).coeff v = D.coeff v + E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma neg_coeff (D : Divisor V) (v : V) : (-D).coeff v = -D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma sub_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D - E).coeff v = D.coeff v - E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma nsmul_coeff (n : ℕ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma zsmul_coeff (n : ℤ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl

/-- The coefficient projection `Divisor V → (V → ℤ)` is injective; hence divisors form an
additive commutative group under pointwise operations. -/
instance : AddCommGroup (Divisor V) :=
  Function.Injective.addCommGroup (Divisor.coeff)
    (fun _ _ h => Divisor.ext h)
    rfl (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)
    (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)

end Divisor

/-- A divisor is **effective** when every coefficient is non-negative. -/
def Effective {V : Type*} (D : Divisor V) : Prop := ∀ v, 0 ≤ D.coeff v

/-! ## Degree -/

section Degree
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V]

/-- The **degree** of a divisor is the sum of its coefficients. -/
def divisorDegree (D : Divisor V) : ℤ := ∑ v, D.coeff v

@[simp] lemma divisorDegree_zero : divisorDegree (0 : Divisor V) = 0 := by
  simp [divisorDegree]

lemma divisorDegree_add (D E : Divisor V) :
    divisorDegree (D + E) = divisorDegree D + divisorDegree E := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_add_distrib]

lemma divisorDegree_neg (D : Divisor V) : divisorDegree (-D) = -divisorDegree D := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_neg_distrib]

end Degree

/-! ## The graph Laplacian (chip-firing operator) -/

section Laplacian
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- The graph Laplacian applied to a firing pattern `f : V → ℤ`.  Firing along `f` moves
chips according to `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`. -/
def lap (f : V → ℤ) : Divisor V := ⟨fun v => ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u)⟩

@[simp] lemma lap_coeff (f : V → ℤ) (v : V) :
    (lap G f).coeff v = ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u) := rfl

-- !-- The empty firing pattern moves no chips: each summand `0 - 0` vanishes. -- !--
@[simp] theorem lap_zero : lap G (0 : V → ℤ) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- A constant firing pattern is in the kernel: every summand `c - c` vanishes. -- !--
theorem lap_const (c : ℤ) : lap G (fun _ => c) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- Additivity: `(f+g)v - (f+g)u = (f v - f u) + (g v - g u)`, then split the sum. -- !--
theorem lap_add (f g : V → ℤ) : lap G (f + g) = lap G f + lap G g := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.add_coeff, Pi.add_apply, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Negation: `lap` is `ℤ`-linear, so it commutes with pointwise negation. -- !--
theorem lap_neg (f : V → ℤ) : lap G (-f) = - lap G f := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.neg_coeff, Pi.neg_apply, ← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Every Laplacian has degree zero, by antisymmetry of `f v - f u` under the symmetric
--     adjacency relation: the swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` on adjacent ordered pairs negates each
--     summand yet preserves the index set, forcing `X = -X`. -- !--
theorem lap_deg_zero (f : V → ℤ) : divisorDegree (lap G f) = 0 := by
  unfold divisorDegree
  simp only [lap_coeff]
  have key : (∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u))
      = ∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f u - f v) := by
    rw [Finset.sum_sigma', Finset.sum_sigma']
    apply Finset.sum_nbij' (fun x => (⟨x.2, x.1⟩ : Σ _ : V, V)) (fun x => ⟨x.2, x.1⟩)
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl

# Summary of changes for run 84becd05-0dac-4116-91e5-3f77f178924f
Created a finished, self-contained Lean file `Catalog/Geometry/FiniteSpecialization.lean` proving the finite reconstruction theorem from the specialization relation. It compiles cleanly against the project's mathlib with no `sorry` and no extra axioms, reusing mathlib's existing machinery throughout.

Orientation note: I determined from mathlib that for the lower-set topology the convention is `a ⤳ b ↔ a ≤ b` (`Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le`), so I used the lower-set topology as the "topology generated by a preorder" and stated everything accordingly.

Contents (theorem names reflect what is proved):

1. `isOpen_specializes_down` — for an arbitrary topology, every open set is downward closed under specialization: `IsOpen s → ∀ ⦃a b⦄, a ∈ s → b ⤳ a → b ∈ s` (a restatement of mathlib's `IsOpen.stableUnderGeneralization`).

2. `isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite` — on a `Fintype`, the converse holds, characterizing openness as being downward closed under specialization. # FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Phantom Topologies (Combinatorics)

Cycle-1/2 results live in `Catalog/Speculative/PhantomTopologies.lean`, where we proved that
on a finite carrier the topology is a *phantom* of its specialization preorder:

- `topology_eq_of_specializes_iff` — a topology is determined by the bare `⤳` relation;
- `specPreorder_bijective` — `topology ↦ specialization preorder` is a **bijection**
  `TopologicalSpace α ≃ Preorder α` (the classical "finite spaces = preorders");
- `continuous_iff_specializes` — continuity *is* specialization-monotonicity (morphisms are
  phantoms too);
- `phantom_asymmetry` — the realized preorders are genuinely directional.

The conjectures below are bold, falsifiable next steps. Each comes with a concrete Lean target.

---

## C1. T0 rigidity: phantoms collapse exactly onto partial orders
**Conjecture.** The observation map `specPreorder` restricts to a bijection between the
`T0` topologies on a finite `α` and the **partial orders** on `α`.
**Why plausible.** `specializationOrder` already upgrades the preorder to a partial order under
`T0Space`; antisymmetry is exactly the `T0` (Kolmogorov) condition.
**Lean target.**
```
theorem specPreorder_T0_bijective [Finite α] :
    Function.Bijective
      (fun (t : {t : TopologicalSpace α // @T0Space α t}) => (specialization partial order))
```
A corollary would be a *counting* statement: `#{T0 topologies on Fin n} = #{partial orders on Fin n}`
(OEIS A001035), complementing the full count A000798.

## C2. Homeomorphism is an order-isomorphism of phantoms
**Conjecture.** For finite spaces, `Homeomorph α β` is in natural bijection with order-isomorphisms
of their specialization preorders: `(α ≃ₜ β) ≃ (Specialization α ≃o Specialization β)`.
**Why plausible.** `continuous_iff_specializes` gives the arrow-level dictionary; a homeomorphism is
a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, i.e. a monotone bijection with monotone inverse.
**Lean target.** Build the explicit `Equiv` and prove both round-trips; specialize to deduce that
two finite spaces are homeomorphic iff their preorders are order-isomorphic.

## C3. Connectivity is a phantom (combinatorial connectivity)
**Conjecture.** A finite space is topologically connected **iff** its specialization preorder is
connected as a graph under the comparability relation `x ≤ y ∨ y ≤ x` (zigzag-connected).
**Why plausible.** In an Alexandrov space the minimal open set of `x` is its up-set; topological
components match equivalence classes of the reflexive–symmetric–transitive closure of `≤`.
**Lean target.**
```
theorem connected_iff_preorder_connected [Finite α] [TopologicalSpace α] :
    ConnectedSpace α ↔ (∀ x y : α, Relation.ReflTransGen (fun a b => a ⤳ b ∨ b ⤳ a) x y)
```

## C4. McCord/Möbius bridge: Euler characteristic = Möbius number
**Conjecture.** For a finite `T0` space `X` with specialization poset `P`, the reduced Euler
characteristic of the order complex `Δ(P)` equals the Möbius number `μ(P̂)` of `P` with adjoined
`⊥`/`⊤` — a strict identity between a topological invariant and a purely combinatorial one.
**Why plausible.** This is the finite-space shadow of McCord's weak-homotopy equivalence
`|Δ(P)| ≃ X`; the alternating face count of `Δ(P)` is the order-complex Euler characteristic, which
Philip Hall's theorem identifies with a Möbius value.
**Lean target.** Define `orderComplex P` (chains of `P`), its Euler characteristic, and prove the
identity for the partial order produced by `specializationOrder`.

## C5. Asymptotic dominance of asymmetric phantoms
**Conjecture.** The fraction of topologies on `Fin n` that are `T0` (genuinely asymmetric phantoms,
cf. `phantom_asymmetry`) tends to `1` as `n → ∞`; equivalently `A000798(n) / A001035(n) → 1`.
**Why plausible.** A random preorder is asymptotically almost surely a partial order, since the
number of nontrivial inseparability classes is negligible for large `n`.
**Lean target.** A clean intermediate, fully finitary milestone: prove the *exact* small-case
counts agree with the phantom bijection, e.g. that there are exactly `4` topologies and `4`
preorders on a 2-element type, and exactly `3` of them are `T0`, by transporting the count along
`specPreorder_bijective`.

concept.mathematical_framing: A Sudoku puzzle is a constraint satisfaction problem on a 9x9 grid. The 'spectral gap' of a Sudoku puzzle is the gap between the two largest eigenvalues of the transition matrix of the Markov chain that randomly swaps two compatible entries. The spectral gap determines the mixing time: the number of swaps needed to generate a uniformly random solution. Conjecture: the spectral gap of a Sudoku puzzle undergoes a phase transition at the critical density d_c = 17/81 (the density of the minimal number of clues, 17, divided by 81). For puzzles with fewer than 17 clues, the spectral gap is large (the Markov chain mixes quickly, meaning there are many solutions). For puzzles with exactly 17 clues, the spectral gap is minimal (the chain mixes slowly, meaning solutions are hard to find). For puzzles with more than 30 clues, the spectral gap is zero (the chain is reducible, meaning the puzzle has a unique solution and no swaps are possible). Conjecture: the spectral gap lambda_1 - lambda_2 of the Sudoku Markov chain satisfies: lambda_1 - lambda_2 > epsilon for d < 17/81 (many solutions, fast mixing), lambda_1 - lambda_2 ~ 0 for d ~ 17/81 (critical point, slow mixing), and the chain is absorbing for d > 30/81 (unique solution, no mixing). Test: compute the spectral gap for Sudoku puzzles with varying numbers of clues and verify the phase transition. Impact: Sudoku has a spectral gap phase transition. The hardness of the puzzle is determined by the gap, not by the number of clues.

/-
  # The Order-`n` Sudoku Constraint Graph

  We formalize the finite combinatorics of the order-`n` Sudoku constraint graph.

  A *cell* of the order-`n` Sudoku board is a quadruple `(a, b, r, c)` of elements
  of `Fin n`.  We interpret it so that:

  * `(a, r)` is the *global row*  (band `a`, row `r` inside the band),
  * `(b, c)` is the *global column* (stack `b`, column `c` inside the stack),
  * `(a, b)` is the *box*.

  Two distinct cells are adjacent in `sudokuGraph n` iff they share a global row,
  a global column, or a box.

  ## Main results

  * `sudokuGraph_adj_iff` — unfolded description of adjacency.
  * `card_cell` — there are `n ^ 4 = (n ^ 2) ^ 2` cells.
  * `sudokuGraph_degree` — every vertex has degree `3 * n ^ 2 - 2 * n - 1`,
    proved by inclusion–exclusion on the row/column/box neighbourhoods, and
    `sudokuGraph_isRegular` packaging this as regularity.
  * `cellColor` and `sudokuGraph_colorable` — an explicit proper coloring with
    `n ^ 2` colors, hence `Colorable (n ^ 2)`.
  * `rowClique_isNClique` / `colClique_isNClique` — explicit cliques of size `n ^ 2`.
  * `sudokuGraph_chromaticNumber` — the chromatic number equals `n ^ 2`.

  ## A note on the coloring

  The naive color `(a,b,r,c) ↦ (r,c)` suggested by the "value inside a box"
  intuition is **not** a proper coloring: the two distinct cells `(a,b₁,r,c)` and
  `(a,b₂,r,c)` share the global row `(a,r)` (so are adjacent) yet both receive the
  color `(r,c)`.  We therefore use the mixed coloring
  `(a,b,r,c) ↦ (b + r, a + c)` (addition in `Fin n`), which one checks is injective
  on every row, column, and box and hence is a genuine proper coloring with `n ^ 2`
  colors.
-/
import Mathlib

open SimpleGraph Finset

namespace SudokuConstraintGraph

/-- A cell of the order-`n` Sudoku board, written `(a, b, r, c)`. -/
abbrev Cell (n : ℕ) := Fin n × Fin n × Fin n × Fin n

/-! ## The constraint graph -/

/-- The order-`n` Sudoku constraint graph: distinct cells are adjacent iff they
share a global row `(a, r)`, a global column `(b, c)`, or a box `(a, b)`. -/
def sudokuGraph (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Cell n) where
  Adj v w :=
    v ≠ w ∧
      ((v.1 = w.1 ∧ v.2.2.1 = w.2.2.1) ∨
        (v.2.1 = w.2.1 ∧ v.2.2.2 = w.2.2.2) ∨
        (v.1 = w.1 ∧ v.2.1 = w.2.1))
  symm := by
    rintro v w ⟨hvw, h⟩
    refine ⟨hvw.symm, ?_⟩
    rcases h with ⟨h1, h2⟩ | ⟨h1, h2⟩ | ⟨h1, h2⟩
    · exact Or.inl ⟨h1.symm, h2.symm⟩
    · exact Or.inr (Or.inl ⟨h1.symm, h2.symm⟩)
    · exact Or.inr (Or.inr ⟨h1.symm, h2.symm⟩)
  loopless := ⟨fun _v h => h.1 rfl⟩

instance (n : ℕ) : DecidableRel (sudokuGraph n).Adj := by
  intro v w; unfold sudokuGraph; infer_instance

/-- Adjacency in the Sudoku constraint graph, fully unfolded. -/
theorem sudokuGraph_adj_iff (n : ℕ) (v w : Cell n) :
    (sudokuGraph n).Adj v w ↔
      v ≠ w ∧
        ((v.1 = w.1 ∧ v.2.2.1 = w.2.2.1) ∨
          (v.2.1 = w.2.1 ∧ v.2.2.2 = w.2.2.2) ∨
          (v.1 = w.1 ∧ v.2.1 = w.2.1)) :=
  Iff.rfl

/-- Adjacency in coordinates `(a, b, r, c)`. -/
theorem sudokuGraph_adj_iff' (n : ℕ) (a₁ b₁ r₁ c₁ a₂ b₂ r₂ c₂ : Fin n) :
    (sudokuGraph n).Adj (a₁, b₁, r₁, c₁) (a₂, b₂, r₂, c₂) ↔
      (a₁, b₁, r₁, c₁) ≠ (a₂, b₂, r₂, c₂) ∧
        ((a₁ = a₂ ∧ r₁ = r₂) ∨ (b₁ = b₂ ∧ c₁ = c₂) ∨ (a₁ = a₂ ∧ b₁ = b₂)) :=
  Iff.rfl

/-! ## Vertex count -/

/-- There are `n ^ 4 = (n ^ 2) ^ 2` cells. -/
theorem card_cell (n : ℕ) : Fintype.card (Cell n) = (n ^ 2) ^ 2 := by
  simp [Cell, Fintype.card_prod, Fintype.card_fin]; ring

/-! ## Neighbourhood decomposition and degree -/

/-- Cells sharing the global row of `v` (including `v` itself). -/
def rowSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) : Finset (Cell n) :=
  univ.filter (fun w => v.1 = w.1 ∧ v.2.2.1 = w.2.2.1)

/-- Cells sharing the global column of `v` (including `v` itself). -/
def colSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) : Finset (Cell n) :=
  univ.filter (fun w => v.2.1 = w.2.1 ∧ v.2.2.2 = w.2.2.2)

/-- Cells sharing the box of `v` (including `v` itself). -/
def boxSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) : Finset (Cell n) :=
  univ.filter (fun w => v.1 = w.1 ∧ v.2.1 = w.2.1)

theorem card_rowSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) : (rowSet n v).card = n ^ 2 := by
  convert Finset.card_product ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) using 1;
  · refine' Finset.card_bij ( fun w hw => ( w.2.1, w.2.2.2 ) ) _ _ _ <;> simp +decide [ rowSet ];
    aesop;
  · simp +decide [ sq ]

theorem card_colSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) : (colSet n v).card = n ^ 2 := by
  convert Finset.card_product ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) using 1;
  · refine' Finset.card_bij ( fun w hw => ( w.1, w.2.2.1 ) ) _ _ _ <;> simp +decide [ colSet ];
  · simp +decide [ sq ]

theorem card_boxSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) : (boxSet n v).card = n ^ 2 := by
  convert Finset.card_product ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) using 1;
  · refine' Finset.card_bij ( fun w hw => ( w.2.2.1, w.2.2.2 ) ) _ _ _ <;> simp +decide [ boxSet ];
    aesop;
  · simp +decide [ sq ]

theorem card_rowSet_inter_colSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) :
    (rowSet n v ∩ colSet n v).card = 1 := by
  rw [ Finset.card_eq_one ] ; use v ; ext w ; simp +decide [ rowSet, colSet ] ; aesop;

theorem card_rowSet_inter_boxSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) :
    (rowSet n v ∩ boxSet n v).card = n := by
  -- The intersection of rowSet and boxSet is the set of cells in the same row and box as v.
  have h_inter : rowSet n v ∩ boxSet n v = Finset.image (fun c => (v.1, v.2.1, v.2.2.1, c)) (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)) := by
    ext ⟨a, b, r, c⟩; simp [rowSet, boxSet];
    tauto;
  rw [ h_inter, Finset.card_image_of_injective ] <;> norm_num [ Function.Injective ]

theorem card_colSet_inter_boxSet (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) :
    (colSet n v ∩ boxSet n v).card = n := by
  have h_inter : colSet n v ∩ boxSet n v = Finset.image (fun r => (v.1, v.2.1, r, v.2.2.2)) (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)) := by
    ext ⟨ a, b, r, c ⟩ ; simp +decide [ colSet, boxSet ] ; aesop;
  rw [ h_inter, Finset.card_image_of_injective ] <;> norm_num [ Function.Injective ]

theorem card_triple_inter (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) :
    (rowSet n v ∩ colSet n v ∩ boxSet n v).card = 1 := by
  by_contra h;
  exact h ( Finset.card_eq_one.mpr ⟨ v, by ext w; simp +decide [ rowSet, colSet, boxSet ] ; aesop ⟩ )

/--
Three-set inclusion–exclusion, in additive form to avoid `ℕ` subtraction.
-/
theorem card_union3 {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (A B C : Finset α) :
    (A ∪ B ∪ C).card + (A ∩ B).card + (A ∩ C).card + (B ∩ C).card =
      A.card + B.card + C.card + (A ∩ B ∩ C).card := by
  have := Finset.card_union_add_card_inter ( A ∪ B ) C;
  have := Finset.card_union_add_card_inter A B; ( have := Finset.card_union_add_card_inter ( A ∩ C ) ( B ∩ C ) ; ( simp_all +decide [ Finset.inter_left_comm, Finset.inter_comm, Finset.inter_assoc ] ; ) );
  rw [ show C ∩ ( A ∪ B ) = ( A ∩ C ) ∪ ( B ∩ C ) by ext; aesop ] at * ; linarith

/--
The neighbour finset of `v` is the union of the row, column, and box sets,
with `v` itself removed.
-/
theorem neighborFinset_eq (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) :
    (sudokuGraph n).neighborFinset v =
      (rowSet n v ∪ colSet n v ∪ boxSet n v).erase v := by
  ext w; simp [rowSet, colSet, boxSet];
  grind +locals

/--
Inclusion–exclusion value of the union, additive form.
-/
theorem card_union_rcb (n : ℕ) (v : Cell n) :
    (rowSet n v ∪ colSet n v ∪ boxSet n v).card + 2 * n + 1 = 3 * n ^ 2 + 1 := by
